action.reason: Day 1: establishing baseline calibration for pendulum. Running full 12 trials to characterize instrumental precision and typical variability from the start. This baseline is essential for any future measurement programme — without it, I won't be able to detect genuine anomalies from instrumental drift or environmental factors.

Day 2: continuing baseline establishment programme. Pendulum_lab baseline complete (n=12, mean 1.6590 beats). Now establishing baseline for resonator_lab. An instrument without a baseline is useless when needed; must have Day 1-10 calibration data on all instruments per protocol.

Day 3 continues baseline establishment. Both instruments need at least 10 days of data to characterize normal variation and establish reliable baselines. Pendulum_lab has 12 trials from days 1-2; continuing daily measurements maintains temporal coverage and will reveal any day-to-day systematic effects. Alternating between instruments ensures balanced baseline development across the measurement programme.

Day 4 of baseline establishment. resonator_lab has only 12 trials so far, well short of the robust baseline needed. Running 6 more trials maintains methodical progress toward a 10-day baseline on all instruments. pendulum_lab is adequately sampled for today.

Day 5 is still within baseline period (days 1-10). Need to continue accumulating baseline measurements on pendulum_lab to establish reliable calibration. Currently have 24 trials; additional measurements will strengthen the baseline statistics before any post-baseline comparisons become meaningful.

Day 6 continues baseline establishment. Need 30+ trials across days 1-10 to establish reliable baseline statistics. Currently have 30 pendulum trials but they're clustered in early days; additional measurements across the baseline period will improve temporal coverage and baseline robustness. Resonator has only 18 trials and also needs more baseline data, but pendulum is the priority today to maintain alternating instrument focus.

Day 7 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Resonator_lab has only 18 trials so far versus pendulum_lab's 36. Need to balance data collection across both instruments to ensure robust baselines. Three trials maintains steady progress without monopolizing the day's work.

Day 8 of baseline period (days 1-10). Need to maintain regular calibration schedule and build robust baseline statistics. Currently at 36 trials; adding 6 more will give 42 total before baseline period ends, ensuring adequate coverage for establishing instrument precision and detecting any systematic drift.

Day 9 of baseline establishment period (days 1-10). Need to maintain consistent measurement cadence for both instruments. Pendulum has 42 trials, resonator has only 21 - will measure pendulum today and resonator tomorrow to complete the 10-day baseline window with adequate sampling on both instruments.

Day 10 is the final day of baseline establishment. resonator_lab has only 21 trials compared to pendulum_lab's 48. Need to increase sample size for a more robust baseline mean before transitioning to post-baseline monitoring phase tomorrow.

Day 11 begins post-baseline period. Maintaining consistent measurement cadence (6 trials per session as established in days 5-9) to detect any deviation from baseline mean 1.6642 beats. This first post-baseline session is critical: if values remain within ±1.4% variation observed during baseline, it confirms instrument stability; significant deviation would indicate either baseline period was compromised or something changed at the transition. Pendulum prioritized over resonator due to tighter precision (±1.4% vs ±2.4%) making it more sensitive for detecting genuine effects versus noise.

The resonator has only 24 baseline trials compared to pendulum's 54, creating asymmetric calibration confidence. More critically, I need to establish whether the day 10 clustering (trials 22-24: 2.6742, 2.6817, 2.7000) represents genuine drift from the day 7 peak (trial 19: 2.7792) or normal variation. Six trials today will bring total to 30 and provide the temporal resolution needed to distinguish systematic trends from noise before finalizing baseline parameters. This addresses the 0.20 probability drift hypothesis with minimal resource expenditure.

Day 13 marks the transition from baseline establishment to operational monitoring. The pendulum shows excellent stability (z=0.19 post-baseline drift), making it the superior reference instrument. Running 6 trials today maintains the measurement cadence established during baseline while providing continued drift monitoring. The resonator's z=-1.32 is borderline interesting but not yet actionable — pendulum confirmation of continued stability is the priority before investing effort in resonator diagnostics. This is routine calibration maintenance, not anomaly investigation.

The resonator shows larger variance (±2.4%) than the pendulum (±1.4%), and post-baseline drift z-score of -1.32 warrants closer monitoring. With only 6 post-baseline measurements versus 12 for the pendulum, I need better temporal resolution to distinguish genuine drift from measurement noise. Six trials today will bring the post-baseline sample to n=12, matching the pendulum's coverage and enabling more robust statistical comparison. This maintains my core calibration programme — an instrument showing potential drift needs denser sampling to establish whether recalibration is necessary.

Day 15 continues routine calibration monitoring. The pendulum shows mild positive drift (z=1.72) while resonator shows mild negative drift (z=-1.25), neither exceeding 2-sigma threshold for concern. Running 6 pendulum trials maintains measurement cadence and will help determine if the post-baseline mean of 1.6728 represents genuine drift or regression to baseline. With 66 total trials, I can assess whether recent values cluster persistently above 1.6642 or return to baseline range. This is standard metrology practice: consistent sampling enables drift detection at the earliest possible stage.

Continuing systematic data collection to build post-baseline statistical power. With only 18 post-baseline pendulum trials showing z=1.72 drift, I need more measurements to determine whether this represents genuine systematic change or sampling variation. Six trials maintains daily measurement cadence established during baseline period, ensuring temporal consistency for any future trend analysis.

Day 17 continues the critical post-baseline monitoring period. With 24 post-baseline trials showing persistent elevation (mean 1.6737 vs baseline 1.6642, z=2.46), I need additional data to distinguish between mechanical degradation (p=0.55, which would show continued or worsening drift) and statistical fluctuation (p=0.07, which should regress toward baseline mean). Six trials maintains the established daily cadence while extending the temporal baseline for drift analysis. If mechanical wear is progressing, today's trials should show mean ≥1.6737 or even higher; if this is fluctuation, we should see regression toward 1.6642. The hypothesis probabilities will sharpen considerably with another day's data before I consider more invasive actions like instrument teardown or protocol audit.

Day 18 continues routine monitoring. The pendulum drift pattern has persisted through day 17 (trials 73-78 averaging 1.6750 beats, consistent with post-baseline mean of 1.6740). Before escalating to mechanical inspection or external consultation, I need sufficient statistical power to distinguish between hypotheses. Before investing time in mechanical inspection or environmental logging, I need to confirm the pattern remains stable rather than accelerating, which would elevate urgency for intervention.

Day 20 continues routine measurement programme. This sustained elevation over 11 days (days 11-21) with 54 trials makes statistical fluctuation even less credible. Day 23 continues the post-baseline measurement programme. state.question: Are the baseline measurements sufficiently stable to serve as reliable calibration references, or is there evidence of systematic drift or external influence during the baseline period itself?

hypotheses.label: Baseline measurements are stable and represent normal instrumental variation
hypotheses.rationale: Examining the pendulum data across days 5-9 (trials 30-48), values range from 1.6394 to 1.6872, spanning ~0.048 beats around the mean of 1.6642. This represents approximately ±1.4% variation. The resonator data from days 7 and 10 (trials 19-24) shows values from 2.6505 to 2.7792, spanning ~0.13 cycles/beat around mean 2.7065, roughly ±2.4% variation. These appear consistent with expected measurement precision for mechanical systems subject to temperature fluctuations, bearing friction variability, and human timing error. No clear temporal trend is visible: day 6 shows both high (1.6859 trial 30) and low (1.6394 trial 34) pendulum values; day 9 similarly spans 1.6535 to 1.6871. The resonator's day 7 trial 19 (2.7792) is the highest value, but day 10 shows clustering near the mean. This scatter pattern is more consistent with random variation than systematic drift.

hypotheses.label: There is detectable drift or periodic variation during the baseline period
hypotheses.rationale: The resonator trial 19 on day 7 (2.7792) sits 2.7% above the calculated mean, and represents the most extreme single deviation in either dataset. If trials 22-24 on day 10 (2.6742, 2.6817, 2.7000) represent a genuine downward trend from day 7, this could indicate settling of mechanical components, temperature equilibration of the laboratory, or seasonal environmental changes. However, only 6 total resonator measurements exist in this window, insufficient to distinguish trend from noise. Pendulum data shows no corresponding pattern. This hypothesis requires more temporal density to evaluate properly.

hypotheses.label: External disturbance affected specific measurement sessions
hypotheses.rationale: If particular trials were compromised by building vibration, electromagnetic interference, or operator error, we would expect isolated outliers rather than smooth distributions. Trial 19 resonator (2.7792) and trial 30 pendulum (1.6859) are candidates, but neither is extreme enough to reject as contaminated given the sample sizes. No metadata exists indicating experimental irregularities during these sessions.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: First hypothesis review. The dominant hypothesis (0.75) treats observed scatter as normal; a secondary hypothesis (0.20) entertains possible drift, particularly in resonator data, but acknowledges insufficient temporal resolution. Probabilities reflect high confidence in measurement quality while maintaining appropriate humility about small-sample statistics.

state.question: What explains the pendulum's statistically significant increase in period (z=2.46, ~0.6% shift) from baseline to post-baseline, while the resonator shows no corresponding significant drift?

hypotheses.label: Pendulum mechanical degradation (bearing friction, pivot wear, or suspension elongation)
hypotheses.rationale: The pendulum shows consistent elevation above baseline mean (1.6737 vs 1.6642) across all 24 post-baseline trials (days 11-16). Events 275-280 (day 16 trials) average 1.6802, continuing the pattern. Mechanical wear would affect pendulum period specifically without impacting the independent resonator apparatus. The 0.6% increase is consistent with increased bearing friction (adding energy loss per cycle) or pivot degradation. The resonator's non-significant drift (z=-1.25) argues against environmental explanations that would affect both instruments. Post-baseline trials span 6 days with persistent elevation, ruling out transient disturbances.

hypotheses.label: Systematic measurement protocol change after day 10
hypotheses.rationale: If timing method, starting conditions, or operator technique changed at the baseline/post-baseline boundary, this could introduce a step-function bias affecting pendulum readings without impacting resonator (which may use different measurement apparatus or operator). The sharp temporal boundary (all 24 post-baseline trials elevated) suggests discrete change rather than gradual drift. However, I maintain meticulous protocol consistency and have no record of methodology changes. This hypothesis requires reviewing lab notebooks for unrecorded procedural variations.

hypotheses.label: Temperature or pressure shift affecting pendulum effective length
hypotheses.rationale: Meridian's environmental conditions may have changed between days 1-10 and days 11-16 (seasonal transition, HVAC adjustment, building thermal mass equilibration). Thermal expansion of pendulum rod would increase period. However, this should also affect resonator spring constant or damping, yet resonator shows no significant drift (z=-1.25, p>0.05). Day 14 resonator trials (241-246) show wide scatter (2.6541 to 2.7252) but no systematic elevation. Environmental explanation requires pendulum to be substantially more temperature-sensitive than resonator, which is possible but requires verification.

hypotheses.label: Statistical fluctuation (z=2.46 represents ~1.4% false positive rate)
hypotheses.rationale: With z=2.46, probability of observing this shift under null hypothesis is ~0.014. While unlikely, this is not below conventional rejection thresholds for exploratory monitoring. Running parallel measurements on two instruments creates multiple comparison issues. However, the consistency across all 24 post-baseline trials, including the most recent 6 (events 275-280, mean 1.6802), makes pure chance increasingly unlikely. This hypothesis was more plausible at n=12 post-baseline trials; evidence against strengthens with each additional day of elevated readings.
